checks.name: Bundle integrity
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema -- bundle_integrity range_mapping; cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --doc -- schema::PinnedBundle::load
checks.output: 18 integration tests pass (15 under bundle_integrity, 3 under range_mapping) plus the 2 PinnedBundle::load doctests. The digest is now derived from the document instead of taken on trust. (1) SHA-256 is implemented in rust/crates/automonique-protocol/src/digest.rs (369 lines, no dependency, no unsafe; the crate's Cargo.toml still has no [dependencies] section and the workspace Cargo.lock is byte-identical). It is measured against the four published FIPS 180-4 / RFC 6234 vectors (empty -> e3b0c442..., "abc" -> ba7816bf..., the 448-bit case -> 248d6a61..., the 896-bit multi-block case -> cf5b16a7...), the 1,000,000-character vector (cdc76e5c9914fb9281a1c7e284d73e67f1809a48a497200e046d39ccc7112cd0), 16 lengths of 'a' spanning every padding boundary (1, 54, 55, 56, 57, 63, 64, 65, 111, 112, 119, 120, 127, 128, 129, 1000), all 256 byte values (40aff2e9...), and streaming equivalence: a 1000-byte non-uniform pattern fed in every chunk size from 1 to 70 yields the same digest as the one-shot call. The boundary and pattern expectations were produced by an independent implementation (CPython hashlib.sha256) and are recorded as fixtures; the five vectors named first are the published ones. (2) SchemaDocument::canonical_bytes defines the exact bytes hashed: a self-naming tag, then every section preceded by its element count and every string by its byte length as big-endian u64. Tests observe that the baseline plus nine single-part mutations of it (renamed field, retyped field, requiredness flipped, enum sensitivity changed, enum value added, message kind added, endpoint added, unmodelled value reshaped, unmodelled key renamed) produce ten distinct digests, that message kinds ["ab","c"] and ["a","bc"] differ, that unmodelled ("ab","c") and ("a","bc") differ, that the same name as a message kind and as an endpoint differ, and that construction order does not affect the bytes. (3) PinnedBundle::load now takes four parameters; the computed_digest parameter is gone, not ignored. Passing a caller-computed digest fails to compile: verified standalone with rustc 1.93.1 on a probe file, which reports exactly one error, 'error[E0061]: this function takes 4 arguments but 5 arguments were supplied ... unexpected argument #4 of type &std::string::String'. The doctest is annotated ```compile_fail,E0061``` and is paired with a passing example that differs only by that extra argument; note honestly that stable rustdoc does NOT enforce the error-code annotation (changing it to E0308 left the doctest passing), so the standalone rustc run above is what pins the reason. (4) load parses the declared digest into a typed Sha256Digest (canonical sha256:<64 lowercase hex> only; empty, 'sha256:aaaa', bare hex, 'sha1:...' and uppercase hex are all refused with SchemaError::DigestMalformed), computes the document's digest, and returns SchemaError::DigestMismatch{declared, computed} naming both when they disagree; the tests assert the exact declared/computed pair for a bundle carrying another document's digest and for a pin that was not updated after the document gained a field. (5) PinnedBundle stores no digest at all: it holds provider, version range and document, and digest() recomputes from the document, so a loaded bundle whose digest disagrees with its content is unrepresentable rather than merely refused once. (6) The test this row previously cited as proof of the hole is gone: range_mapping::overlapping_ranges_for_one_provider_are_a_conflict_at_load now loads four genuinely distinct documents under their own digests, and range_mapping::distinct_bundles_carry_distinct_documents_and_distinct_digests asserts the four digests are distinct; loading four copies of one document under four different digests is no longer writable. (7) Negative controls: 13 single-point mutations were applied one at a time, measured, and reverted (script kept out of the tree). Every one was detected: dropping the declared-versus-computed comparison (2 tests fail), making digest() stop deriving from the document (2), corrupting one round constant (6), moving the padding length offset from 56 to 55 (8), writing the length suffix in bytes rather than bits (6), dropping the w[i-7] term from the schedule (6), making update stop counting bytes (6), making the parser fold uppercase hex (2), dropping the requiredness byte (1), dropping the enum-sensitivity byte (1), dropping the string length prefix (1), dropping the section element counts (1), and reverting the range-mapping fixtures to one shared document (1). The suite returned to 18 passed / 0 failed after restore.

checks.name: Range mapping
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema range_mapping
checks.output: 3 tests pass, re-measured after the bundles were rebuilt on real digests. Inserting a second bundle for provider 'codex' covering 3..=7 while 1..=3 is already registered is refused with SchemaError::OverlappingRanges{provider: "codex"}, so ranges that merely touch at one version are a conflict at load rather than a silent choice; a disjoint 4..=7 for the same provider and any range for a different provider ('opencode' 1..=3) are accepted. Each of those four bundles now carries a different document, and their four digests are asserted distinct. Lookup never guesses: with codex pinned at 1..=3 and 10..=12, version 5 (between the two ranges), version 99 (above both) and an unknown provider all resolve to Resolution::Unpinned, while version 2 resolves to the bundle whose digest equals the low document's digest and version 12 to the one matching the high document's. Resolution has exactly two variants, so there is no nearest-neighbour outcome to return.

checks.name: Verdict exhaustiveness
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema verdict_exhaustiveness
checks.output: 2 tests pass. classify() returns a Verdict holding one VerdictKind, so exactly one of the three is structurally guaranteed; the test drives one document per verdict against the same baseline and observes Compatible (identical documents), Breaking (a removed field) and Unclassifiable (a changed unmodelled construct), and every kind has a non-empty stable spelling. Across the whole suite the classifier's five input constructs each have covering cases: fields (removed, added optional, added required, type changed, requirement tightened, requirement relaxed), enums (removed, added, value removed, value added under each sensitivity, sensitivity changed), message kinds (added, removed), endpoints (added, removed) and unmodelled entries (changed, removed, added). The verdict distribution over the fixture corpus, counted as expected-verdict occurrences across the 23 classify() call sites in tests/schema.rs, is 6 Compatible, 12 Breaking and 3 Unclassifiable; the classification tests were not touched by the digest work and the call-site count is unchanged. Stated plainly: exhaustiveness is a property of the return type plus this enumeration of covering cases, not a machine-checked proof over the construct space.

checks.name: Unclassifiable is preserved
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema unclassifiable_is_preserved
checks.output: 2 tests pass. A document that adds an optional field (purely additive) while also reshaping an unmodelled vendor block classifies Unclassifiable, not Compatible, and names at least one change, so an additive change cannot launder an unmodelled one. Precedence is Breaking over Unclassifiable over Compatible: a document that removes a field and reshapes the unmodelled block classifies Breaking, which is the more actionable answer. The collapse the row forbids is unreachable in the code: the Compatible branch is taken only when both the breaking and the unclassifiable lists are empty.

checks.name: Evidence completeness
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema evidence_completeness
checks.output: 3 tests pass. A Breaking verdict names the path that broke ('turn.id') with the reason 'field removed'. A Compatible verdict names what was added: exactly one change, path 'turn.label', reason 'optional field added'. Emptying the document entirely yields Breaking with non-empty evidence, and changing only the unmodelled entry yields Unclassifiable with non-empty evidence, so neither of those two kinds is ever evidence-free. Verdict has private fields and classify() is its only constructor, so a verdict carrying no reason for its kind cannot be fabricated, though that privacy is not covered by a compile-fail test. One documented exception: classifying a document against itself returns Compatible with empty evidence, which the source comments acknowledge and the test asserts; when nothing changed there is no changed path to name.

checks.name: Additive rules
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema additive_rules
checks.output: 5 tests pass, one per rule direction. Compatible: a new optional field, a new message kind ('turn_steered'), a new endpoint ('/v1/runs') and a relaxed requirement (required to optional, evidence reason 'field became optional'), plus a new value in a read-only enum from the security_enum_rule module. Breaking: a new required field ('turn.tenant'), a type change (string to integer), a tightened requirement (optional to required), a removed message kind and a removed endpoint. Each case was classified against the same baseline document, and the reasons recorded by the classifier are the ones the rule table names.

checks.name: Security enum rule
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema security_enum_rule
checks.output: 3 tests pass. Adding 'allow_always' to the security-sensitive approval.decision enum classifies Breaking with the reason 'value added to a security-sensitive enum', matching the R1-03 rule that such an enum rejects unknown values, so a change that would make an existing reader fail closed is not compatible merely because it is an addition. Adding 'hibernated' to the read-only run.state enum classifies Compatible. Removing a value from either enum is Breaking, and changing an enum's sensitivity is Breaking with the reason 'enum sensitivity changed'.

checks.name: Determinism
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test schema determinism
checks.output: 2 tests pass. Classifying the same pair of documents nine times (one baseline plus eight repeats) yields verdicts that compare equal, including their evidence vectors, so a diff of two runs is empty. Order independence is proved at both ends: two documents built from the same parts in forward and reversed order compare equal, because SchemaDocument::new sorts fields and enums by path and sorts and dedups kinds, endpoints and unmodelled entries; and the verdicts derived from each compare equal. Evidence is canonically ordered: the returned change paths were already in sorted order, and classify() sorts and dedups the evidence before returning it. The digest inherits the same property: bundle_integrity::document_encoding::the_digest_does_not_depend_on_the_order_parts_were_supplied_in observes identical canonical_bytes and identical digests for forward and reversed construction.

checks.output: Re-measured at this HEAD, and the previous wording is corrected: the crate now DOES contain a hash implementation, and that is the point of this attempt. automonique-protocol still declares no dependencies at all (its Cargo.toml has no [dependencies] section) and forbids unsafe_code, dbg_macro, todo and unimplemented at the crate level; src/digest.rs is pure safe Rust over in-memory slices and opens nothing. The grep (recorded here with -E, since the previously recorded command used alternation without -E and therefore matched nothing) returns exactly one hit across the whole crate, std::net::{Ipv4Addr, Ipv6Addr} in primitives.rs, which are address parsing types and open no socket; there is no std::process, no std::fs, no Command::new, no SystemTime or Instant, and no env:: use. digest.rs imports only core::fmt, core::str::FromStr and std::error::Error; schema.rs imports only core::fmt, std::error::Error and the crate's own codec and digest modules. Documents are supplied as values by the caller: no function in either module takes a path or a URL. The entire suite builds and runs with --offline.

notes:
Both rows that were open are now closed by measurement, not by rewording. Bundle integrity: the crate hashes the document itself (src/digest.rs, SHA-256 from FIPS 180-4, no dependency, no unsafe), SchemaDocument::canonical_bytes defines the bytes hashed with an injective length-prefixed encoding, PinnedBundle::load parses the declared pin into a typed digest and refuses a document that does not produce it, the computed_digest parameter was deleted rather than ignored, and PinnedBundle stores no digest so it cannot drift from its document after loading. Quality: 1046 passed / 0 failed at this HEAD. Every new behaviour was negative-controlled: 13 mutations applied one at a time, each observed to fail the suite, each reverted, and the suite observed green again afterwards.

What is still qualified. (1) The compile-fail doctest's ```compile_fail,E0061``` annotation is not enforced by stable rustdoc — swapping the code to E0308 left the doctest passing — so the reason it fails was pinned by running the same snippet through rustc standalone, which reported exactly one error, E0061. (2) The SHA-256 vectors that are actually published are the empty, "abc", 448-bit, 896-bit and one-million-'a' cases; the 16 padding-boundary lengths, the all-256-byte-values case and the 1000-byte pattern were cross-checked against CPython hashlib rather than against a published table, and the test comments say so. (3) The privacy of PinnedBundle's fields — the reason no caller can assemble a bundle without going through load — rests on Rust's module privacy and is not covered by its own compile-fail test, matching the existing qualification recorded for Verdict. (4) Unchanged from the previous evidence: verdict exhaustiveness rests on the return type plus an enumeration of covering cases rather than a machine-checked proof; a Compatible verdict is empty when the two documents are identical; the corpus is entirely synthetic, since no provider binary was invoked and no R0-06 capture was checked in; and the full classifier rule table the Compatibility section asks for exists only as the covering cases listed under Additive rules, Security enum rule and Unclassifiable is preserved, not as a checked-in table. (5) A gap in the contract's prose that no verification row covers, recorded rather than silently closed: the Pipeline contract says a pinned bundle carries the exact binary version, the binary digest and the capture method, and PinnedBundle carries none of those three — it holds the provider, the inclusive version range and the document, and derives the document digest. Closing that would change PinnedBundle's shape and is not demanded by any row in the check table, so it was left alone rather than folded into this attempt.
